197.title: Pauri 22, sound: paataalaa paataal
197.howItsDone: Pauri 22 is recited in the morning Japji Sahib; its opening line, with its doubled words, is one of the most rhythmic in the bani.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the hour creation began. Your line was only the maker knows. Did you say I don't know, once, and let it be fine? Today, from when to where. Day one hundred ninety-seven.

Stand in an elevator in a very tall building and look at the buttons. Basement, sub-basement, parking level three. And above you, floor after floor, up to a number you can barely read. Now imagine the buttons never end, in either direction. Below the lowest basement, another. Above the top floor, another sky. Yesterday Japji asked when. Today it asks where, and how far. And the first line of Pauri 22 sounds like that endless elevator.
screen: `AN ELEVATOR, BASEMENT TO SKY.` → `THE BUTTONS NEVER END.` → `FROM WHEN TO WHERE.`

segments.voice: Here's the first line of Pauri 22, in the original: paataalaa paataal lakh aagaasaa aagaas. Let's take it apart. Paataal, paa-TAAL: the lower worlds, the regions under the earth. In old Indian cosmology, there were said to be many of them, one below another. Paataalaa paataal: underworlds below underworlds. Lakh: a hundred thousand, the word Indians still use for big numbers, as in five lakh rupees. Aagaas, aa-GAAS: sky, the heavens, from the Sanskrit akasha. Aagaasaa aagaas: skies beyond skies. So: underworlds below underworlds, and hundreds of thousands of skies above skies. Now listen to how it's built. Each half doubles its word: paataalaa paataal, aagaasaa aagaas. The first form of the word, with the extra aa, reaches, and the second one lands. It sounds like going down a staircase, step after step, and then climbing into the sky, step after step. The line doesn't describe the size of the universe. It makes you feel it in your mouth. It also carries on what the countless stanzas started, but now in a direction. Asankh was about number. This is about depth and height: down, down, up, up. The rest of the stanza will ask whether anyone has found the end, and whether it could ever be written. That's tomorrow. Today, just the elevator, and the sound of it: paataalaa paataal.
screen: `PAATAAL — THE LOWER WORLDS.` · `LAKH — A HUNDRED THOUSAND.` · `AAGAAS — SKY, SKIES BEYOND SKIES.` · `DOWN, DOWN, UP, UP.` · then, large: `PAATAALAA PAATAAL.`

segments.voice: Say the first line aloud: paataalaa paataal, lakh aagaasaa aagaas. On the first half, let your attention sink down, into your seat, into the floor, into the ground beneath. On the second half, let it rise, up through the ceiling, into the open sky. Say it twice more. Then sit quietly between the two, the ground below and the sky above. The bell holds the time.
Pauri 22. It opens paataalaa paataal, lakh aagaasaa aagaas: underworlds below underworlds, hundreds of thousands of skies above skies.
Your line: paataalaa paataal. Today, when you ride an elevator or climb stairs, let the line play, and imagine the steps never ending. Day one hundred ninety-seven.

198.title: Pauri 22, meaning: worlds beyond worlds
198.hook: underworlds beyond underworlds, skies beyond skies; if it could be written it would be, but the writing runs out (Japji 22)
198.howItsDone: Pauri 22 is recited in the morning Japji Sahib; Sikhs often cite its closing, that only the One knows Himself, when speaking of the limits of human description.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sound of Pauri 22. Your line was paataalaa paataal: underworlds below underworlds, skies beyond skies. Today, what happens to anyone who tries to measure them. Day one hundred ninety-eight.

Picture someone trying to write down every star. They start with a notebook. Then a shelf of notebooks. Then a library. Years go by; their handwriting gets shaky. And the sky hasn't gotten any smaller. At some point, the one writing runs out before the stars do. Pauri 22 draws that picture, and it isn't sad about it. It's almost relieved. It says: this was never going to fit on paper.
screen: `WRITING DOWN EVERY STAR.` → `A NOTEBOOK, A SHELF, A LIBRARY.` → `THE WRITER RUNS OUT FIRST.`

segments.voice: After underworlds below underworlds and skies beyond skies, Pauri 22 goes on, in paraphrase. People searched and searched for the farthest edge, and grew tired. The Vedas say this one thing: there's no end to find. The books of the Semitic traditions, the Kateb, speak of eighteen thousand worlds; but at the root there is one source. Notice what Guru Nanak does there. He gathers the scriptures of the two great communities around him, Hindu and Muslim, and hears them both pointing the same direction: past counting, toward one. He doesn't set them against each other. Then the line behind today's carry. If there were an account, the stanza says, you could write it down. But the account perishes in the writing. In the original: lekhaa hoe ta likheeai lekhai hoe vinaas. Lekhaa is an account, a ledger, a tally. Vinaas is destruction, perishing. Commentators read it two ways. The account itself falls apart before it's done. Or the one writing it perishes before the account is finished. Either way: the writing runs out. And the stanza ends, in paraphrase: Nanak says, call Him great; He alone knows Himself. That's not giving up. It's the same move Japji has been making since Pauri 12: no pen for this. It's the right size of a human being, standing under the sky. We can say great. We can't write the whole ledger. And there's something freeing in that. You don't have to finish the account. You can just look up.
screen: `THEY SEARCHED, AND GREW TIRED.` · `THE VEDAS, THE KATEB, ONE SOURCE.` · `LEKHAA HOE TA LIKHEEAI.` · `CALL HIM GREAT; HE KNOWS HIMSELF.` · then, large: `THE WRITING RUNS OUT.`

segments.voice: If you can, look at the sky for a minute: through a window, from a doorway, or step outside. If you can't see it, close your eyes and picture the widest sky you remember. Don't try to name or count what's there. Just look, and let it be bigger than you. When the minute is up, close your eyes and sit with the size of it. The bell holds the time.
Pauri 22. Worlds beyond worlds; the searchers grow tired; if it could be written, it would be, but the writing runs out. Call Him great.
Your line: the writing runs out. Today, when a list or a worry keeps growing, stop writing it for a moment and look up. Day one hundred ninety-eight.

199.title: Pauri 23, sound: saalaahee saalaah
199.hook: saalaahee saalaah etee surat na paaeeaa
199.tomorrow: Pauri 23, meaning: the ant who remembers
199.howItsDone: Pauri 23 is recited in the morning Japji Sahib; praise, saalaah, is at the center of Sikh worship, sung as kirtan in gurdwaras every day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, worlds beyond worlds. Your line was the writing runs out. Did you stop a growing list, once, and look up? Today, the ones who praise. Day one hundred ninety-nine.

Think of the biggest fan you know. The friend who can tell you every stat of her team from the last twenty years, or the neighbor who has seen his favorite band sixty times. They praise and praise. And yet, if you asked them to explain what it is about that music, why it moves them the way it does, they'd stumble. Praising something and fully grasping it aren't the same. Pauri 23 opens with the people who praise, and a gentle, honest line about what they still don't know.
screen: `THE BIGGEST FAN YOU KNOW.` → `THEY PRAISE AND PRAISE.` → `PRAISING ISN'T GRASPING.`

segments.voice: Here's the first line of Pauri 23 in the original: saalaahee saalaah etee surat na paaeeaa. Let's take it slowly. Saalaah, saa-LAAH: praise. We met it in Pauri 19: akharee saalaah, through letters, praise. Saalaahee, saa-laa-HEE: the praisers, those who praise. So saalaahee saalaah: the praisers praise. The same root twice, like an echo. Etee: this much, so much. Surat: awareness, understanding. You know that word; it was our word on day one hundred eighty-four, the waking attention that trust brings. Na paaeeaa: have not obtained, have not reached. Put together: the praisers praise, but have not reached an understanding of how great. Hear the music of it. Saalaahee saalaah, soft and flowing, the long aa sounds like breath going out. Then etee surat na paaeeaa, the line tips over, as if it's shrugging. Notice the tone. This isn't criticism of the people who praise. Japji is praise from start to finish. It's the same honesty that runs all through these stanzas: no pen for this, the writing runs out, only the Maker knows. Even the ones who praise the most haven't grasped the size of it. And that's not a failure. Praise doesn't need a complete understanding to be real. The rest of the stanza, tomorrow, gives a picture of that: rivers, the sea, and a very small ant. Today, the sound. Saalaahee saalaah.

segments.voice: Say the first line aloud: saalaahee saalaah, etee surat na paaeeaa. Once slowly, letting the long aa sounds breathe out. Twice more, softer each time. Then sit, and let one thing you love come to mind. Praise it silently, without trying to explain it. Let it stay bigger than your understanding. The bell holds the time.
Pauri 23. It opens saalaahee saalaah, etee surat na paaeeaa: the praisers praise, but haven't grasped how great.
Your line: saalaahee. Today, praise one person out loud, specifically, without needing to explain everything they mean to you. Day one hundred ninety-nine.

200.title: Pauri 23, meaning: the ant who remembers
200.hook: rivers flow into the sea without knowing its size; kings with mountains of wealth are not equal to an ant who remembers (Japji 23)
200.howItsDone: Pauri 23 is recited in the morning Japji Sahib; Sikhs practice simran, remembering the Name through the day, and often quote the ant of this stanza to say remembrance matters more than wealth or rank.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sound of Pauri 23. Your line was saalaahee: the praisers praise, but haven't grasped how great. Did you praise one person out loud? Today, the same stanza's meaning, and a very small hero. Day two hundred.

Have you ever watched an ant for a whole minute? Get down low on a sidewalk and follow one. It carries a crumb twice its size, loses it, finds it, goes around a pebble, keeps going. It never looks up at the buildings or the traffic. It isn't impressed by anything. It just keeps its one thread. Now picture a king on a golden throne, with vaults of treasure and armies at the gate. If someone asked you which one matters more, you'd probably laugh. Pauri 23 gives an answer that stops the laugh.
screen: `WATCH AN ANT FOR A MINUTE.` → `IT KEEPS ITS ONE THREAD.` → `THE ANT, OR THE KING?`

segments.voice: The stanza began yesterday: the praisers praise, but haven't grasped how great. Now it gives two pictures. The first, in paraphrase: rivers and streams pour into the ocean, but they don't know how big the ocean is. They just flow in. That's us, praising. We're part of something we can't measure, and we pour into it anyway. The second picture turns the world's scale upside down. Kings and emperors, with kingdoms as vast as oceans and wealth piled like mountains, are not equal to an ant, if the ant does not forget the One in its heart. The word for ant is keeRee, one of the smallest living things anyone can see. And the condition is simple: je tis manahu na veesarahi, if it does not forget Him in its mind. The whole weight of the scale rests on that one condition. The Sikh word for that is simran, remembrance, keeping the Name in mind through the day. Pauri 23 says a creature the size of a grain of rice, if it remembers, outweighs every palace. It's not saying wealth is evil. Plenty of Sikhs run businesses and work hard. It's saying what the scale is actually measuring. Not size. Not money. Not how much you understand; the river doesn't understand the sea. Just whether you remember. That's the end of this stretch of Japji: bhareeai hath, as you sow, teerath tap, only the Maker knows, worlds beyond worlds, the praisers, and now the ant. Two hundred days in, it's a good picture to carry. Small, steady, remembering.
screen: `RIVERS DON'T KNOW THE SEA.` · `KINGS WITH MOUNTAINS OF WEALTH.` · `AN ANT WHO DOESN'T FORGET.` · `THE SCALE MEASURES REMEMBERING.` · then, large: `BE THE ANT.`

segments.voice: Watch something small. A leaf moving, a drop on a glass, a bug on the windowsill, a crumb, a flicker of light. If there's nothing, watch the small rise and fall of your own breath. Give it your whole attention, the way the ant gives its whole attention to one crumb. Each time your mind wanders off to bigger things, come back to the small one. The bell holds the time.
Pauri 23. Rivers pour into a sea they can't measure; kings with mountains of wealth don't equal an ant that remembers.
Your line: be the ant. Today, pick one small moment, a doorway, a sip of water, a red light, and use it to remember. Day two hundred.

201.title: Pauri 24, sound: ant na siftee
201.hook: ant na siftee kahan na ant
201.tomorrow: Pauri 24, meaning: no end to praise
201.howItsDone: Pauri 24 is recited in the morning Japji Sahib; its repeated word ant, end, gives the stanza a steady, rolling rhythm that many Sikhs know by heart.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ant who remembers. Your line was be the ant. Did one small moment become a reminder? Today, a word that sounds just like it and means something else entirely. Day two hundred one.

Here's a small gift from language. Yesterday the hero was an ant. Today, the first word of Pauri 24 is also ant, spelled the same in English letters. But in Punjabi, ant means end. The finish, the limit, the last page. And this stanza is going to use that word again and again, only to say there isn't one. No end, no end, no end. It's as if the whole stanza is a song about a road with no last mile. Today, just its first line, and the sound of it.
screen: `YESTERDAY, AN ANT.` → `TODAY, ANT MEANS END.` → `NO END, NO END, NO END.`

segments.voice: Here's the first line of Pauri 24 in the original: ant na siftee kahan na ant. Let's take it word by word. Ant, with a short a, UNT: end, limit. Na: no, not. Siftee, SIF-tee: praises, qualities. The word comes from sifat, which reached Punjabi from Arabic and Persian, and means an attribute, a quality worthy of praise. You'll hear the phrase sifat salaah, praise and glory, all through Sikh life. Kahan: saying, telling. So: there's no end to the praises, and no end to the telling of them. Now listen to how the line is shaped. It starts with ant and ends with ant. The word for end is at both ends, like two bookends, and between them the line says there's no end. The shape of the sentence plays against its meaning. That's poetry you can feel even before you understand. The rest of the stanza keeps going the same way, in paraphrase: no end to His works, no end to His giving, no end to seeing, no end to hearing. Line after line, the word ant, and the word na. Guru Nanak is generally described as writing in the everyday speech of his region rather than a classical language, and his words draw on many sources: Punjabi, words from Sanskrit, words from Persian and Arabic, like sifat here. Tomorrow we'll open what the whole stanza means. Today, the sound. Ant na siftee, kahan na ant. End at both ends, and no end in the middle.
screen: `ANT — END, LIMIT.` · `SIFTEE — PRAISES, QUALITIES.` · `ANT AT BOTH ENDS OF THE LINE.` · `WORDS FROM MANY LANGUAGES.` · then, large: `ANT NA SIFTEE.`

segments.voice: Say the first line aloud: ant na siftee, kahan na ant. Feel it start and finish on the same word. Say it twice more, slower. Then sit, and notice the breath. Each breath ends, and another begins, and there's no last one you can feel coming. Rest in that rolling, one breath after another. The bell holds the time.
Pauri 24. It opens ant na siftee, kahan na ant: no end to the praises, no end to their telling. Ant means end.
Your line: ant na siftee. Today, when something good ends, a meal, a song, a talk, whisper the line, and notice what keeps going. Day two hundred one.

202.title: Pauri 24, meaning: no end to praise
202.hook: there is no end to His praise, His works, His gifts; the more is said, the more remains (Japji 24)
202.howItsDone: Pauri 24 is recited in the morning Japji Sahib; Sikhs often quote bahutaa aakheeai bahutaa hoe to say that praise of the One never runs out.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sound of Pauri 24. Your line was ant na siftee: end at both ends, and no end in the middle. Today, what the whole stanza says. Day two hundred two.

You know that feeling when you try to thank someone who really changed your life. A teacher, a grandparent, the friend who got you through the worst year. You say thank you. Then you remember something else they did. Then something else. You write a card, and the card's too small. The more you say, the more there is to say. That isn't a failure of your words. It's a sign of how much there was. Pauri 24 is built on exactly that feeling.
screen: `THANKING SOMEONE WHO CHANGED YOU.` → `ONE MORE THING, ONE MORE.` → `THE CARD IS TOO SMALL.`

segments.voice: Pauri 24 is a long chain of the word ant, end. In paraphrase: no end to the praises, no end to telling them. No end to His works, no end to His giving. No end to seeing, no end to hearing. His mind's purpose can't be known to its end. The created world can't be known to its end, nor its near shore, nor its far one. So many cry out wanting to find its limits, and its limits can't be found. No one knows this end. And then the line behind today's carry, in the original: bahutaa aakheeai bahutaa hoe. The more is said, the more there is. Think about how strange that is. Usually saying things uses them up. You tell a story and it's told. Here it's the opposite. Every word of praise opens more to praise. Then the stanza climbs, in paraphrase: great is the Master, high His place, and higher than high is His Name. Only someone as high as He could know Him. Only He knows how great He is. And the last line: Nanak, the gift comes by the glance of grace. That's the stanza's quiet resting point. We can't reach the end by talking. What we have comes as a gift, through nadar, grace, a word we'll keep meeting in Japji. So the praising never finishes, and that's not a problem to fix. It's what praising something infinite feels like from inside. Like the card that's too small, it tells you how much there was.

When you think you've run out, keep going: find one more thing to notice about it, and one more. See whether the more you say, the more there is. Then let the words stop and sit with what's left over. The bell holds the time.
Pauri 24. No end to the praises, the works, the gifts; the more is said, the more there is; and the gift comes by grace.
Your line: the more remains. Today, thank one person for one thing, then add one more thing, and notice there's still more. Day two hundred two.

203.title: Pauri 25, sound: bahutaa karam
203.tomorrow: Pauri 25, meaning: even hunger is a gift
203.howItsDone: Pauri 25 is recited in the morning Japji Sahib; the giving it describes is echoed in the langar, the free community kitchen in every gurdwara, where anyone is fed.

segments.voice: Yesterday, no end to praise. Your line was the more remains. Did you thank someone, and find there was more to thank them for? Today, the end of a week, and a stanza about giving. Day two hundred three.

Look back at this week. Paataalaa paataal, the endless elevator. The writing runs out. Saalaahee, the praisers who never grasp it all. Be the ant. Ant na siftee, and the more remains. Every day, a way of saying: too big for us. Now picture a grandmother who cooks for everyone who walks through the door. You ask her how much she's made. She laughs. She's never counted. Keeping score isn't how she thinks. Pauri 25 starts with a giver like that.
screen: `THE WEEK: ENDLESS, UNWRITTEN, THE ANT.` → `A GRANDMOTHER WHO COOKS FOR ALL.` → `SHE'S NEVER COUNTED.`

segments.voice: Here's the first line of Pauri 25 in the original: bahutaa karam likhiaa naa jaae. Bahutaa: so much, so great. You heard it yesterday: bahutaa aakheeai bahutaa hoe. Karam: and here's a word to be careful with. It looks like karma, but most Sikh commentators read karam here as a different word, from Persian and Arabic, meaning generosity, kindness, grace. Not what you've done, but what's given to you. Likhiaa: written. Naa jaae: cannot be. So: His generosity is so great it cannot be written down. That's the same honesty as the last few stanzas, the writing runs out, but now about giving. The next line, in paraphrase: the great Giver doesn't have even a sesame seed of greed. There's til again, the sesame seed from Pauri 21. The Giver wants nothing back, not even that much. Listen to the rhythm. Bahutaa karam, two strong beats, a lift. Likhiaa naa jaae, falling softly, like setting something down. It's an easy line to carry. Sikh life is built around that picture of a giver who doesn't count. The langar, the free kitchen in every gurdwara, feeds anyone who comes, of any faith or none, sitting together on the floor, and nobody tallies who ate. Tomorrow we'll hear where the stanza goes, and it goes somewhere surprising, to hunger and pain. Today, just the sound. Bahutaa karam: so much giving it can't be written.
screen: `BAHUTAA — SO MUCH.` · `KARAM — GENEROSITY, GRACE.` · `NOT A SESAME SEED OF GREED.` · `THE LANGAR DOESN'T COUNT.` · then, large: `BAHUTAA KARAM.`

segments.voice: Say the first line aloud: bahutaa karam, likhiaa naa jaae. Once slowly, feeling the lift and the fall. Twice more, softer. Then sit and bring to mind three things you were given this week that you didn't earn: a smile, a meal, a kind word, a sunrise. Don't count them up. Just let them arrive. The bell holds the time.
Pauri 25. It opens bahutaa karam, likhiaa naa jaae: His generosity is so great it cannot be written.
Your line: bahutaa karam. Today, give one thing without keeping score: a coffee, a favor, your time, and don't mention it. Day two hundred three.
